readerTitle: The rival is 3% cheaper. Her empty shelves cost more.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (철물점과 유통업체, 회사 안의 IT팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용 · 개념 배경은 Dixon & Adamson (2011)
insight: 고객이 이미 아는 문제로 경쟁하면 가격 싸움이 된다. 고객이 아직 재지 않은 비용을 보여주면 판단 기준 자체가 바뀐다.
misconception: 좋은 영업은 고객의 말을 잘 듣고 원하는 것을 맞춰 주는 것이다. 고객이 가격을 말하면 가격 문제다.

sources.text: Dixon, M. & Adamson, B. (2011). The Challenger Sale. Portfolio/Penguin. (CEB의 영업 담당자 대규모 조사를 바탕으로, 높은 성과자는 고객에게 그들의 사업에 대해 새로운 것을 가르친다고 주장)
철물점, 유통업체, IT팀 사례와 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 정합성 확인: 베스트셀러 소매 $150,000의 도매 원가는 $150,000 × 60% = $90,000으로 연간 구매액 $100,000 안에 들어갑니다. 품절 시 고객이 대체 상품을 사지 않는다는 단순화 가정이며, 6번 카드에서 이 한계를 밝혔습니다.
Dixon & Adamson(2011)의 내용을 4번 카드에서 일반적으로만 서술했습니다. 조사 규모나 비율 같은 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 원서 표현과 맞는지 확인하세요. 브랜드명 'Challenger'는 본문에 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The rival is 3% cheaper. Her empty shelves cost more.
body: A hardware store owner tells her distributor that a rival is 3% cheaper. She's right about the price.
But she's watching the wrong number. A bigger cost sits in her own aisles, and nobody has added it up.

image.label: A store shelf with a few empty gaps among full rows
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 철물점 진열대에 나사, 테이프, 전구가 가득한데 군데군데 빈 칸이 보임. 빈 칸 위에 작은 물음표 태그. 계산대 쪽에 "3% cheaper"라고 적힌 작은 전단지. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: She'll switch unless you do something.
body: You're the distributor. She buys $100,000 a year from you. The rival delivers once a week. You deliver twice a week, but it costs a bit more.
She says: "Match their price or I'm moving." What's your move?

options.text: Match the 3% to keep the account
options.feedback: You keep her, but you give up $3,000 a year. You also confirm that price is the only thing worth comparing.

options.text: Ask her more about what she needs from a supplier
options.feedback: Good habit, but she'll likely say "lower prices." Customers can't tell you about a cost they've never noticed.

options.text: Show her a cost in her own store that she hasn't measured
options.feedback: This changes what she's comparing. It works only if the cost is real and your offer actually reduces it. Next card shows the math.

cards.title: Add up the empty shelves.
body: Her best sellers from you bring in $150,000 a year at retail. Her own records show they're out of stock about one day in ten. Twice-weekly delivery could cut those gaps by two-thirds.
The saving she asked for is smaller than the loss she couldn't see.

cards.title: Teaching the customer something new
body: **Teaching the customer something new** means showing them a cost, risk or chance in their own business that they hadn't seen, so they judge the options differently.
She came in comparing prices. She leaves comparing profit. Your price didn't change. Her yardstick did.

In *The Challenger Sale* (2011), Matthew Dixon and Brent Adamson drew on a large study of sales reps. They argued that top performers often teach customers something about their business instead of only answering their requests.

image.label: A scale shifting from price tags to profit
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 왼쪽은 "Price per case" 라벨이 붙은 가격표 두 장이 거의 같은 무게. 오른쪽 장면에서는 저울 접시가 "Profit per year"로 바뀌고 한쪽이 확실히 기움. 단순한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Three moves that make the lesson land.
body: A good teaching moment has a shape:
list: **Start with their view:** repeat what they believe, fairly. "Price matters, and they are cheaper."
**Use their numbers:** her sales records, her empty shelves. Not your brochure.
**Lead to your strength:** the hidden cost should be one you're better at fixing than rivals.
cards.callout: If the lesson points to a problem anyone could solve, you've just trained your rival's customer.
cards.softwareNote: A software seller might pull a prospect's own data to show how many hours staff spend retyping orders between two systems. The lesson is about the prospect's week, not the product's features.

cards.title: Teaching can backfire.
body: The math must be true and checkable. Here, some customers facing an empty shelf buy a similar item instead, so the real loss may be smaller. Say so. One inflated number ruins the whole case.
Tone matters too. "You've been doing it wrong" makes people defend themselves. "Here's something stores like yours often miss" invites them in.
And you can't teach what you haven't learned. Ask questions first, then teach.

cards.title: Now you're the IT team asking for budget.
body: You run IT support at a large company. You want to replace 300 aging laptops. The finance director sees only the purchase price and says it can wait another year.
How do you make your case?

options.text: Show the new laptops' speed tests and features
options.feedback: It's about your solution, not her problem. Faster machines sound nice, but nothing here changes how she weighs the cost.

options.text: Use help-desk records to show the staff hours lost to slow, failing machines, priced in salary
options.feedback: Her own company's numbers reveal a cost she isn't tracking. It takes work to gather, but it turns "spend" into "stop losing."

options.text: Point out that similar companies replace laptops every three to four years
options.feedback: Shows the request is normal, which helps. But it doesn't show what waiting costs this company, so it's easy to postpone.

cards.title: Change what the customer is measuring.
body: When a customer compares you on a number you'll lose, find the cost they haven't counted, prove it with their own data, and make sure it's one you fix best.
**Try it today:** list one cost your customers carry but rarely measure. Can you estimate it in dollars from records they already have?
